M0 · Warm-up: Quantum Scattering in One Dimension

Learning goals. After this chapter you should be able to

  • set up a one-dimensional scattering problem with incident, reflected and transmitted waves;
  • use the probability current to prove R+T=1R + T = 1R+T=1;
  • solve the step, the barrier and the well, and recognise tunneling and transmission resonances;
  • estimate tunneling through smooth barriers with the Gamow factor, and apply it to α decay (★);
  • write the one-dimensional S-matrix and its even/odd phase shifts, the bridge to the partial waves
    of Chapter 2;
  • follow a wave packet through a barrier, define the Wigner time delay and explain resonant
    tunneling;
  • use transfer matrices and the split-operator method, and know their pitfalls.

Prerequisites: a first course in quantum mechanics (time-independent Schrödinger equation,
square well, Fourier transforms).

Sources: any quantum-mechanics text for the basics (e.g. Griffiths, ch. 2); Landau & Lifshitz
§25 for barrier transmission; C&H §8.2.1 for the S-matrix language in one dimension. Longer
derivations are collected in the section Detailed derivation at the end of the chapter.

Units in the figures. Formulas are written with ℏ\hbarℏ and mmm. The figures use
ℏ=1\hbar = 1ℏ=1 and 2m=12m = 12m=1: then E=k2E = k^2E=k2, the Schrödinger equation is −ψ′′+Vψ=Eψ-\psi'' + V\psi = E\psi−ψ′′+Vψ=Eψ,
and a packet with wave number kkk moves with velocity v=2kv = 2kv=2k. For a nucleon with lengths in fm,
one energy unit is ℏ2/(2m fm2)=20.7\hbar^2/(2m\,\mathrm{fm}^2) = 20.7ℏ2/(2mfm2)=20.7 MeV and one time unit is
ℏ/(20.7 MeV)≈3.2×10−23\hbar/(20.7\ \mathrm{MeV}) \approx 3.2\times10^{-23}ℏ/(20.7 MeV)≈3.2×10−23 s.

M0.1 Why start in one dimension?

Chapter 2 shows that scattering by a central potential in three dimensions reduces to a set of
radial equations, one for each angular momentum. The s-wave radial equation is a one-dimensional
Schrödinger equation on the half-line r≥0r \ge 0r≥0, with a hard wall at the origin. Everything in this
chapter therefore has a three-dimensional counterpart: transmission and reflection become phase
shifts and S-matrix elements, and tunneling governs α decay and sub-barrier fusion. Resonances and
time delays reappear for quasi-bound nuclear states. One dimension lets us see these ideas without
angular-momentum bookkeeping.

Before solving anything, we should say precisely what a scattering problem asks, because it is a
different question from the one asked for bound states. In a bound-state problem the energy is the
unknown: we look for the energies at which a normalizable solution exists. In a scattering problem
the energy E>0E > 0E>0 is fixed by the beam, every such energy is allowed, and the question is what
comes out. Suppose that the potential V(x)V(x)V(x) approaches constant values V∓V_\mpV∓​ as x→∓∞x \to \mp\inftyx→∓∞.
Far to the left and far to the right the particle is then free, and there the Schrödinger equation
has the plane waves e±ikxe^{\pm ikx}e±ikx as solutions. A particle sent in from the left is described by a
stationary state that contains, on the left, the incident wave together with a reflected wave, and
on the right only a transmitted wave, because nothing is sent in from the right:

ψ(x)→{eikx+r e−ikx,x→−∞,t eik′x,x→+∞,k=2m(E−V−)ℏ,k′=2m(E−V+)ℏ.(M0.1)\psi(x) \to \begin{cases} e^{ikx} + r\,e^{-ikx}, & x \to -\infty,\\[2pt] t\,e^{ik'x}, & x \to +\infty, \end{cases} \qquad k = \frac{\sqrt{2m(E - V_-)}}{\hbar},\quad k' = \frac{\sqrt{2m(E - V_+)}}{\hbar}. \tag{M0.1} ψ(x)→{eikx+re−ikx,teik′x,​x→−∞,x→+∞,​k=ℏ2m(E−V−​)​​,k′=ℏ2m(E−V+​)​​.(M0.1)

The incident wave has unit amplitude, and the reflected amplitude rrr and the transmitted amplitude
ttt are what the potential decides; finding them is the whole problem. Such a state is not
normalizable. It describes a steady beam rather than a single particle. Section M0.7 shows how a
normalizable wave packet is built from these states, and M2 §M2.3 how continuum states are
normalized.

M0.2 Probability current and flux conservation

To interpret ∣r∣2|r|^2∣r∣2 and ∣t∣2|t|^2∣t∣2 as probabilities, we need to know how probability flows. Start from
the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, iℏ ∂tψ=−(ℏ2/2m) ∂x2ψ+Vψi\hbar\,\partial_t\psi = -(\hbar^2/2m)\,\partial_x^2\psi + V\psiiℏ∂t​ψ=−(ℏ2/2m)∂x2​ψ+Vψ,
multiply it by ψ∗\psi^*ψ∗, and subtract the complex conjugate of the result. For a real potential the
two terms containing VVV cancel, and what remains can be written as a derivative:

iℏ ∂∣ψ∣2∂t=−ℏ22m(ψ∗∂2ψ∂x2−ψ ∂2ψ∗∂x2)=−ℏ22m ∂∂x(ψ∗∂ψ∂x−ψ ∂ψ∗∂x).i\hbar\,\frac{\partial|\psi|^2}{\partial t} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\left(\psi^*\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial x^2} - \psi\,\frac{\partial^2\psi^*}{\partial x^2}\right) = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\psi^*\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x} - \psi\,\frac{\partial\psi^*}{\partial x}\right). iℏ∂t∂∣ψ∣2​=−2mℏ2​(ψ∗∂x2∂2ψ​−ψ∂x2∂2ψ∗​)=−2mℏ2​∂x∂​(ψ∗∂x∂ψ​−ψ∂x∂ψ∗​).

The bracket on the right is 2i Im(ψ∗∂xψ)2i\,\mathrm{Im}(\psi^*\partial_x\psi)2iIm(ψ∗∂x​ψ), so this is the continuity
equation

∂∣ψ∣2∂t+∂j∂x=0,j=ℏm Im⁡ ⁣(ψ∗∂ψ∂x),(M0.2)\frac{\partial |\psi|^2}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial j}{\partial x} = 0, \qquad j = \frac{\hbar}{m}\,\operatorname{Im}\!\left(\psi^*\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\right), \tag{M0.2} ∂t∂∣ψ∣2​+∂x∂j​=0,j=mℏ​Im(ψ∗∂x∂ψ​),(M0.2)

with jjj the probability current. It says that probability is neither created nor destroyed,
only moved: the probability inside an interval changes only by the current that flows through its
ends.

In a stationary state ∣ψ∣2|\psi|^2∣ψ∣2 does not change in time, so ∂j/∂x=0\partial j/\partial x = 0∂j/∂x=0 and the
current is the same everywhere. We may therefore evaluate it far to the left and far to the right of
the potential, where (M0.1) holds. On the left,
ψ∗ψ′=ik[1−∣r∣2+r∗e2ikx−r e−2ikx]\psi^*\psi' = ik\left[1 - |r|^2 + r^*e^{2ikx} - r\,e^{-2ikx}\right]ψ∗ψ′=ik[1−∣r∣2+r∗e2ikx−re−2ikx]. The two interference terms are
of the form z−z∗z - z^*z−z∗, so their sum is purely imaginary; multiplied by ikikik it becomes real and drops
out of the imaginary part. What remains is j=(ℏk/m)(1−∣r∣2)j = (\hbar k/m)(1 - |r|^2)j=(ℏk/m)(1−∣r∣2), the incident current minus
the reflected one. On the right only the transmitted wave contributes, j=(ℏk′/m)∣t∣2j = (\hbar k'/m)|t|^2j=(ℏk′/m)∣t∣2.
Equating the two gives

R+T=1,R=∣r∣2,T=k′k ∣t∣2.(M0.3)R + T = 1,\qquad R = |r|^2,\qquad T = \frac{k'}{k}\,|t|^2 . \tag{M0.3} R+T=1,R=∣r∣2,T=kk′​∣t∣2.(M0.3)

The incident flux is shared between reflection and transmission. The factor k′/kk'/kk′/k, the ratio of the
velocities on the two sides, appears because TTT compares fluxes rather than amplitudes: a slower wave
carries less probability per unit time for the same amplitude. It matters whenever the potential is
different on the two sides, as for the step of the next section.

The same conservation law can be stated without reference to time. Up to a constant, jjj is the
Wronskian ψ∗ψ′−ψ∗′ψ\psi^*\psi' - \psi^{*\prime}\psiψ∗ψ′−ψ∗′ψ of the two solutions ψ\psiψ and ψ∗\psi^*ψ∗, and the Wronskian
of any two solutions of the same equation ψ′′=(2m/ℏ2)(V−E)ψ\psi'' = (2m/\hbar^2)(V - E)\psiψ′′=(2m/ℏ2)(V−E)ψ is constant, because its
derivative ψ∗ψ′′−ψ∗′′ψ\psi^*\psi'' - \psi^{*\prime\prime}\psiψ∗ψ′′−ψ∗′′ψ vanishes. This “Wronskian equals flux” idea returns
in Chapter 2 (§2.5), and in Chapter 7, where an absorptive potential makes the current decrease.

M0.3 The potential step

The simplest potential that scatters is a step: V=0V = 0V=0 for x<0x < 0x<0 and V=V0>0V = V_0 > 0V=V0​>0 for x>0x > 0x>0.
Since the potential is constant on each side, the asymptotic form (M0.1) is now the exact solution,
ψ=eikx+re−ikx\psi = e^{ikx} + re^{-ikx}ψ=eikx+re−ikx for x<0x < 0x<0 and ψ=teiqx\psi = te^{iqx}ψ=teiqx for x>0x > 0x>0, with
q=2m(E−V0)/ℏq = \sqrt{2m(E - V_0)}/\hbarq=2m(E−V0​)​/ℏ. The Schrödinger equation is of second order and the potential is
finite, so ψ′′\psi''ψ′′ has at most a jump at x=0x = 0x=0, and ψ\psiψ and ψ′\psi'ψ′ must both be continuous
there. These two conditions, 1+r=t1 + r = t1+r=t and k(1−r)=qtk(1 - r) = qtk(1−r)=qt, are linear equations for the two
unknowns. Substituting t=1+rt = 1 + rt=1+r into the second gives k−kr=q+qrk - kr = q + qrk−kr=q+qr, hence

r=k−qk+q,t=2kk+q,R=(k−qk+q)2,T=4kq(k+q)2.(M0.4)r = \frac{k - q}{k + q},\qquad t = \frac{2k}{k + q},\qquad R = \left(\frac{k - q}{k + q}\right)^2,\qquad T = \frac{4kq}{(k + q)^2}. \tag{M0.4} r=k+qk−q​,t=k+q2k​,R=(k+qk−q​)2,T=(k+q)24kq​.(M0.4)

As a check, R+T=[(k−q)2+4kq]/(k+q)2=1R + T = [(k - q)^2 + 4kq]/(k + q)^2 = 1R+T=[(k−q)2+4kq]/(k+q)2=1, as (M0.3) requires.

When the energy lies above the step, a classical particle would always pass, and yet R>0R > 0R>0: the
particle is reflected by the sudden change of wave number, not by a turning point. The reflection
grows to R=1R = 1R=1 as E→V0+E \to V_0^+E→V0+​, where q→0q \to 0q→0, and vanishes as E→∞E \to \inftyE→∞, where q→kq \to kq→k.
Nothing in the derivation used the sign of V0V_0V0​, so the same formula holds for a downward step: a
quantum particle can be reflected by a cliff. This reflection is a wave effect of the abruptness of
the change. It becomes much weaker when the potential changes smoothly over a distance longer than the
wavelength, which will matter for the diffuse (Woods–Saxon) surfaces of nuclei.

When the energy lies below the step, the wave number on the right becomes imaginary,
q=iκq = i\kappaq=iκ with κ=2m(V0−E)/ℏ\kappa = \sqrt{2m(V_0 - E)}/\hbarκ=2m(V0​−E)​/ℏ, and the transmitted wave te−κxte^{-\kappa x}te−κx decays.
This evanescent wave penetrates the step over a depth 1/κ1/\kappa1/κ but carries no current, because
ψ∗ψ′\psi^*\psi'ψ∗ψ′ is real for it. Accordingly the reflection is total: r=(k−iκ)/(k+iκ)r = (k - i\kappa)/(k + i\kappa)r=(k−iκ)/(k+iκ) is
a ratio of complex conjugates, so ∣r∣=1|r| = 1∣r∣=1. Its phase still carries information. Writing
r=−e2ikdr = -e^{2ikd}r=−e2ikd, as for a hard wall placed at x=dx = dx=d, gives d=arctan⁡(k/κ)/kd = \arctan(k/\kappa)/kd=arctan(k/κ)/k, which approaches
1/κ1/\kappa1/κ deep below the step: the wave is reflected as if from a wall inside the step, at about the
penetration depth. This is a first glimpse of the time delays of §M0.8. Figure M0.1 shows both
regimes. Below the step, the incident and reflected waves form a standing wave with ∣ψ∣2|\psi|^2∣ψ∣2
between 0 and 4. Above it, the standing-wave pattern has little contrast, since R=0.058R = 0.058R=0.058 at
E=1.6V0E = 1.6V_0E=1.6V0​.

M0.4 Tunneling through a barrier

M0.4.1 The rectangular barrier

The step has shown what happens at a single edge: below its top, a particle is reflected completely,
although its wave function leaks into the forbidden region over a depth 1/κ1/\kappa1/κ. A barrier has a
second edge at a finite distance aaa. If aaa is not much larger than 1/κ1/\kappa1/κ, the evanescent wave
reaches the far side with a non-zero amplitude, and some probability can emerge there. To find out how
much, let the potential be V0V_0V0​ for 0<x<a0 < x < a0<x<a and zero elsewhere, and consider E<V0E < V_0E<V0​ first. In
each of the three regions the Schrödinger equation has constant coefficients, so its solutions are
exponentials:

ψ(x)={eikx+r e−ikx,x<0,C eκx+D e−κx,0<x<a,t eikx,x>a,k=2mEℏ,κ=2m(V0−E)ℏ.\psi(x) = \begin{cases} e^{ikx} + r\,e^{-ikx}, & x < 0,\\[2pt] C\,e^{\kappa x} + D\,e^{-\kappa x}, & 0 < x < a,\\[2pt] t\,e^{ikx}, & x > a, \end{cases} \qquad k = \frac{\sqrt{2mE}}{\hbar},\quad \kappa = \frac{\sqrt{2m(V_0 - E)}}{\hbar}. ψ(x)=⎩⎪⎪⎪⎨⎪⎪⎪⎧​eikx+re−ikx,Ceκx+De−κx,teikx,​x<0,0<x<a,x>a,​k=ℏ2mE​​,κ=ℏ2m(V0​−E)​​.

Inside the barrier we must keep the growing exponential eκxe^{\kappa x}eκx as well as the decaying one,
because the region is finite and nothing forbids it. The four unknowns rrr, CCC, DDD and ttt are fixed
by four conditions: ψ\psiψ and ψ′\psi'ψ′ must be continuous at x=0x = 0x=0 and at x=ax = ax=a.

It is easiest to start on the right, where only one wave is present. The two conditions at x=ax = ax=a,
Ceκa+De−κa=teikaCe^{\kappa a} + De^{-\kappa a} = te^{ika}Ceκa+De−κa=teika and κ (Ceκa−De−κa)=ik teika\kappa\,(Ce^{\kappa a} - De^{-\kappa a}) = ik\,te^{ika}κ(Ceκa−De−κa)=ikteika,
can be solved for the interior amplitudes:

C=t eika2(1+ikκ)e−κa,D=t eika2(1−ikκ)eκa.C = \frac{t\,e^{ika}}{2}\Big(1 + \frac{ik}{\kappa}\Big)e^{-\kappa a},\qquad D = \frac{t\,e^{ika}}{2}\Big(1 - \frac{ik}{\kappa}\Big)e^{\kappa a}. C=2teika​(1+κik​)e−κa,D=2teika​(1−κik​)eκa.

At x=0x = 0x=0 the conditions read 1+r=C+D1 + r = C + D1+r=C+D and ik(1−r)=κ(C−D)ik(1 - r) = \kappa(C - D)ik(1−r)=κ(C−D). We do not need rrr, so
we eliminate it: dividing the second equation by ikikik and adding it to the first gives
2=(1−iκ/k) C+(1+iκ/k) D2 = (1 - i\kappa/k)\,C + (1 + i\kappa/k)\,D2=(1−iκ/k)C+(1+iκ/k)D. Inserting CCC and DDD, the products of brackets are
2±i(k/κ−κ/k)2 \pm i(k/\kappa - \kappa/k)2±i(k/κ−κ/k), and the exponentials combine into hyperbolic functions:

t eika=1cosh⁡κa−i2(kκ−κk)sinh⁡κa.t\,e^{ika} = \frac{1}{\cosh\kappa a - \frac{i}{2}\big(\frac{k}{\kappa} - \frac{\kappa}{k}\big)\sinh\kappa a} . teika=coshκa−2i​(κk​−kκ​)sinhκa1​.

The waves on the two sides have the same wave number, so T=∣t∣2T = |t|^2T=∣t∣2. With
cosh⁡2κa=1+sinh⁡2κa\cosh^2\kappa a = 1 + \sinh^2\kappa acosh2κa=1+sinh2κa and the identity
1+14(kκ−κk)2=(k2+κ2)24k2κ2=V024E(V0−E)1 + \frac14\big(\frac{k}{\kappa} - \frac{\kappa}{k}\big)^2 = \frac{(k^2 + \kappa^2)^2}{4k^2\kappa^2} = \frac{V_0^2}{4E(V_0 - E)}1+41​(κk​−kκ​)2=4k2κ2(k2+κ2)2​=4E(V0​−E)V02​​
(because k2+κ2=2mV0/ℏ2k^2 + \kappa^2 = 2mV_0/\hbar^2k2+κ2=2mV0​/ℏ2), the transmission probability becomes

T=[1+V02 sinh⁡2κa4E(V0−E)]−1,κ=2m(V0−E)ℏ.(M0.5)T = \left[1 + \frac{V_0^2\,\sinh^2\kappa a}{4E(V_0 - E)}\right]^{-1}, \qquad \kappa = \frac{\sqrt{2m(V_0 - E)}}{\hbar}. \tag{M0.5} T=[1+4E(V0​−E)V02​sinh2κa​]−1,κ=ℏ2m(V0​−E)​​.(M0.5)

T=[1+V02 sin⁡2qa4E(E−V0)]−1,q=2m(E−V0)ℏ.(M0.6)T = \left[1 + \frac{V_0^2\,\sin^2 qa}{4E(E - V_0)}\right]^{-1}, \qquad q = \frac{\sqrt{2m(E - V_0)}}{\hbar}. \tag{M0.6} T=[1+4E(E−V0​)V02​sin2qa​]−1,q=ℏ2m(E−V0​)​​.(M0.6)

A square well of depth V0V_0V0​ is simply a barrier of negative height, so replacing V0V_0V0​ by −V0-V_0−V0​ in
(M0.6) gives its transmission without further work:

T=[1+V02 sin⁡2qa4E(E+V0)]−1,q=2m(E+V0)ℏ.(M0.7)T = \left[1 + \frac{V_0^2\,\sin^2 qa}{4E(E + V_0)}\right]^{-1}, \qquad q = \frac{\sqrt{2m(E + V_0)}}{\hbar}. \tag{M0.7} T=[1+4E(E+V0​)V02​sin2qa​]−1,q=ℏ2m(E+V0​)​​.(M0.7)

These three formulas contain the two central phenomena of the chapter. Below the top, (M0.5) is never
zero: the particle tunnels through a region that classical mechanics forbids, with a probability
that, as the next subsection shows, falls off exponentially with κa\kappa aκa. Above the top, (M0.6) and
(M0.7) do not simply approach 1. They oscillate, and they reach T=1T = 1T=1 exactly when sin⁡qa=0\sin qa = 0sinqa=0,
that is, when the barrier or the well holds a whole number of half-wavelengths. Figure M0.2 shows RRR
and TTT for the step, a barrier and a well. The closed forms agree with the general transfer-matrix

M0.4.2 Opaque barriers and the Gamow factor

For a thick or high barrier, κa≫1\kappa a \gg 1κa≫1, the hyperbolic sine in (M0.5) is dominated by its
growing exponential, sinh⁡κa≈eκa/2\sinh\kappa a \approx e^{\kappa a}/2sinhκa≈eκa/2, and the 1 in the bracket becomes
negligible. The bracket is then V02e2κa/16E(V0−E)V_0^2e^{2\kappa a}/16E(V_0 - E)V02​e2κa/16E(V0​−E), and its inverse is

T≈16 EV0(1−EV0)e−2κa.(M0.8)T \approx 16\,\frac{E}{V_0}\left(1 - \frac{E}{V_0}\right)e^{-2\kappa a} . \tag{M0.8} T≈16V0​E​(1−V0​E​)e−2κa.(M0.8)

The exponential controls everything. The amplitude of the evanescent wave falls by a factor
e−κae^{-\kappa a}e−κa across the barrier, and the probability by its square, so doubling the width roughly
squares the already small transmission (Fig. M0.3(a)). To get a feeling for the numbers, take a
nucleon (mc2=939mc^2 = 939mc2=939 MeV) 20 MeV below the top of a barrier 3 fm wide. Then
κ=2mc2(V0−E)/ℏc=2⋅939⋅20/197.3 fm−1=0.98 fm−1\kappa = \sqrt{2mc^2(V_0 - E)}/\hbar c = \sqrt{2\cdot939\cdot20}/197.3\ \mathrm{fm}^{-1} = 0.98\ \mathrm{fm}^{-1}κ=2mc2(V0​−E)​/ℏc=2⋅939⋅20​/197.3 fm−1=0.98 fm−1
and e−2κa=2.8×10−3e^{-2\kappa a} = 2.8\times10^{-3}e−2κa=2.8×10−3. The prefactor in (M0.8) is at most 4, so the nucleon gets
through at most about once in a hundred tries.

Real barriers are not rectangular. The Coulomb barrier of a nucleus falls off like 1/r1/r1/r, and the
barrier that two nuclei must cross in order to fuse is the smooth sum of Coulomb repulsion and nuclear
attraction. To treat a smooth barrier, cut it into thin slices of width dxdxdx. Each slice acts as a
rectangular barrier with its own local κ(x)=2m[V(x)−E]/ℏ\kappa(x) = \sqrt{2m[V(x) - E]}/\hbarκ(x)=2m[V(x)−E]​/ℏ, and when the barrier is
opaque each slice attenuates the wave by e−κ(x) dxe^{-\kappa(x)\,dx}e−κ(x)dx. Multiplying these attenuations, and
ignoring both the prefactors and the reflections between slices, gives the Gamow factor

T≈e−2G,G=1ℏ∫x1x22m [V(x)−E]  dx,(M0.9)T \approx e^{-2G},\qquad G = \frac{1}{\hbar}\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\sqrt{2m\,[V(x) - E]}\;dx , \tag{M0.9} T≈e−2G,G=ℏ1​∫x1​x2​​2m[V(x)−E]​dx,(M0.9)

where the integral runs between the classical turning points x1x_1x1​ and x2x_2x2​, at which V=EV = EV=E. This is
the WKB result, which Chapter 5 derives properly. Its exponent is right; the prefactor, which our
slicing argument cannot give, is close to 1 for a smooth, opaque barrier.

The formula must fail near the barrier top. There the turning points merge and G→0G \to 0G→0, so (M0.9)
predicts complete transmission, whereas a wave that arrives exactly at the top of a smooth barrier is
about half reflected; above the top it predicts no reflection at all. A better formula, due to Kemble,
is T=1/(1+e2G)T = 1/(1 + e^{2G})T=1/(1+e2G). It reduces to e−2Ge^{-2G}e−2G for an opaque barrier and gives T=12T = \frac12T=21​ at the
top. For a parabolic barrier, V(x)=VB−12mω2x2V(x) = V_B - \tfrac12 m\omega^2x^2V(x)=VB​−21​mω2x2, the Gamow integral can be done in
closed form. The turning points lie at ±xt\pm x_t±xt​, with 12mω2xt2=VB−E\tfrac12 m\omega^2x_t^2 = V_B - E21​mω2xt2​=VB​−E, and

M0.4.3 ★ Application: α decay and the Geiger–Nuttall law

The Gamow factor had its first triumph in nuclear physics. In 1928 Gamow, and independently Gurney
and Condon, explained α decay as tunneling, with a model of striking simplicity. An α particle is
assumed to be preformed inside the parent nucleus, where it bounces back and forth with velocity vvv,
so that it hits the surface, at radius RRR, about v/2Rv/2Rv/2R times per second. At each hit it may tunnel
through the Coulomb barrier 2Zde2/r2Z_de^2/r2Zd​e2/r of the daughter nucleus (ZdZ_dZd​ is the daughter’s charge), with
probability e−2Ge^{-2G}e−2G. The decay rate is therefore the knocking rate times the penetrability,
λ=(v/2R) e−2G\lambda = (v/2R)\,e^{-2G}λ=(v/2R)e−2G, and the half-life is t1/2=ln⁡2/λt_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambdat1/2​=ln2/λ. Because the α particle is
emitted in an s wave, the barrier problem is one-dimensional in rrr, and for a pure Coulomb barrier the
Gamow integral (M0.9) can be done in closed form (derivation D.1):

G=2μQℏ b[arccos⁡x−x(1−x)],b=2Zde2Q,x=Rb,(M0.12)G = \frac{\sqrt{2\mu Q}}{\hbar}\,b\left[\arccos\sqrt{x} - \sqrt{x(1-x)}\right], \qquad b = \frac{2Z_de^2}{Q},\quad x = \frac{R}{b}, \tag{M0.12} G=ℏ2μQ​​b[arccosx​−x(1−x)​],b=Q2Zd​e2​,x=bR​,(M0.12)

where QQQ is the decay energy, μ\muμ the reduced mass, and bbb the outer turning point, at which the
Coulomb energy equals QQQ.

The law that Geiger and Nuttall had found empirically in 1911 follows from the limit of a small
nucleus. For R≪bR \ll bR≪b the bracket tends to π/2−2x\pi/2 - 2\sqrt{x}π/2−2x​, and the leading term of the exponent is
2G≈2πZde22μ/Q /ℏ2G \approx 2\pi Z_de^2\sqrt{2\mu/Q}\,/\hbar2G≈2πZd​e22μ/Q​/ℏ, which is 2πη2\pi\eta2πη with η\etaη the Sommerfeld parameter of
the emitted α particle (derivation D.1). The logarithm of the half-life is therefore nearly linear in
Zd/QZ_d/\sqrt{Q}Zd​/Q​. That is the Geiger–Nuttall law. It also explains why the half-lives are so
sensitive to the decay energy: QQQ enters an exponent, so a change of a few MeV changes the half-life
by many orders of magnitude.

Figure M0.4 tests the model on 15 even–even emitters, with R=1.2 (Ad1/3+41/3)R = 1.2\,(A_d^{1/3} + 4^{1/3})R=1.2(Ad1/3​+41/3) fm and no
free parameters. The half-lives range from 0.29 μs (²¹²Po) to 1.4×10101.4\times10^{10}1.4×1010 years (²³²Th),
24 orders of magnitude, yet the model is within a factor of 5 of the data in all cases but one:
²¹⁰Po, where it is 50 times too fast. ²¹⁰Po has the magic neutron number N=126N = 126N=126. The α particle is
less likely to be preformed at a closed shell, which is nuclear structure that a pure tunneling
model leaves out.

measured (dots) and Gamow model (circles), with a straight-line fit to the data. QαQ_\alphaQα​ from
atomic-mass differences; masses and half-lives from the AME2020/NUBASE2020 evaluations with later

M0.5 The square well: transmission resonances

A classical particle crosses an attractive well without hindrance, so one might expect a well to
transmit everything. Equation (M0.7) shows that this is not so.
As E→0E \to 0E→0, the wave number qqq inside the well tends to the finite value 2mV0/ℏ\sqrt{2mV_0}/\hbar2mV0​​/ℏ, so
sin⁡2qa\sin^2qasin2qa stays finite while the factor 1/E1/E1/E in the bracket diverges. The transmission then behaves
as T≈4E(E+V0)/(V02sin⁡2qa)T \approx 4E(E + V_0)/(V_0^2\sin^2qa)T≈4E(E+V0​)/(V02​sin2qa), which vanishes linearly in EEE: slow particles are
reflected almost completely, even by a well. Yet whenever qa=nπqa = n\piqa=nπ the sine vanishes and the well
becomes perfectly transparent, T=1T = 1T=1. This is the Ramsauer–Townsend effect, first seen as the
near-transparency of noble-gas atoms to slow electrons.

The explanation is interference. The wave is partly reflected at each edge of the well. At the first
edge it passes from the slow region into the fast one, at the second from the fast region into the
slow one, so by (M0.4) the two reflected amplitudes have opposite signs. They therefore cancel when the
round trip inside the well adds a whole number of wavelengths, 2qa=2πn2qa = 2\pi n2qa=2πn, exactly as in a
Fabry–Pérot interferometer. For the well of Fig. M0.2© (in units ℏ=2m=1\hbar = 2m = 1ℏ=2m=1, V0=1V_0 = 1V0​=1, a=4a = 4a=4)
the condition q=nπ/aq = n\pi/aq=nπ/a gives the resonances at E=(nπ/a)2−V0=1.47E = (n\pi/a)^2 - V_0 = 1.47E=(nπ/a)2−V0​=1.47 and 4.554.554.55. In three
dimensions the same effect appears when an s-wave phase shift passes through a multiple of π\piπ
(Chapter 2).

M0.6 The one-dimensional S-matrix

So far the particle always came from the left. In general, waves can arrive from both sides, and
since the Schrödinger equation is linear, the outgoing waves must depend linearly on the incoming
ones. Call aLa_LaL​ and aRa_RaR​ the amplitudes of the waves that come in from the left and from the right,
and bLb_LbL​ and bRb_RbR​ those of the outgoing waves on the left and on the right (we take V−=V+V_- = V_+V−​=V+​, so
that all waves have the same kkk). Then

(bLbR)=S(aLaR),S=(rt′tr′),(M0.13)\begin{pmatrix} b_L \\ b_R \end{pmatrix} = S \begin{pmatrix} a_L \\ a_R \end{pmatrix}, \qquad S = \begin{pmatrix} r & t' \\ t & r' \end{pmatrix}, \tag{M0.13} (bL​bR​​)=S(aL​aR​​),S=(rt​t′r′​),(M0.13)

where the primed amplitudes refer to incidence from the right. Two general principles restrict this
matrix, and both reappear for the S-matrices of every later chapter.

The first is flux conservation. For arbitrary incoming amplitudes, the incoming flux is
(ℏk/m)(∣aL∣2+∣aR∣2)(\hbar k/m)(|a_L|^2 + |a_R|^2)(ℏk/m)(∣aL​∣2+∣aR​∣2) and the outgoing flux is (ℏk/m)(∣bL∣2+∣bR∣2)(\hbar k/m)(|b_L|^2 + |b_R|^2)(ℏk/m)(∣bL​∣2+∣bR​∣2), and by
§M0.2 they are equal. In matrix notation, a†S†S a=a†aa^\dagger S^\dagger S\,a = a^\dagger aa†S†Sa=a†a for every vector aaa,
which is possible only if S†S=1S^\dagger S = 1S†S=1: the S-matrix is unitary. Unitarity means that the
columns of SSS are orthonormal, ∣r∣2+∣t∣2=1|r|^2 + |t|^2 = 1∣r∣2+∣t∣2=1, ∣t′∣2+∣r′∣2=1|t'|^2 + |r'|^2 = 1∣t′∣2+∣r′∣2=1 and r∗t′+t∗r′=0r^*t' + t^*r' = 0r∗t′+t∗r′=0. The
last condition gives ∣r∣ ∣t′∣=∣t∣ ∣r′∣|r|\,|t'| = |t|\,|r'|∣r∣∣t′∣=∣t∣∣r′∣, and together with the first two it implies ∣r∣=∣r′∣|r| = |r'|∣r∣=∣r′∣
and ∣t∣=∣t′∣|t| = |t'|∣t∣=∣t′∣: a barrier reflects equally from both sides, however asymmetric its shape.

The second principle is time reversal. For a real potential, if ψ\psiψ solves the Schrödinger
equation, so does ψ∗\psi^*ψ∗. Complex conjugation turns eikxe^{ikx}eikx into e−ikxe^{-ikx}e−ikx, so it exchanges
incoming and outgoing waves: the conjugate solution has incoming amplitudes b∗b^*b∗ and outgoing
amplitudes a∗a^*a∗, and must therefore obey a∗=S b∗a^* = S\,b^*a∗=Sb∗. Combined with b=S ab = S\,ab=Sa, this gives
a∗=SS∗a∗a^* = SS^*a^*a∗=SS∗a∗ for every aaa, so SS∗=1SS^* = 1SS∗=1. Since unitarity already says S−1=S†S^{-1} = S^\daggerS−1=S†, it
follows that S∗=S†S^* = S^\daggerS∗=S†, that is, ST=SS^{\rm T} = SST=S: the S-matrix is symmetric, and in
particular t=t′t = t't=t′.

A third simplification comes from symmetry of the potential. If V(−x)=V(x)V(-x) = V(x)V(−x)=V(x), parity is conserved,
and every solution splits into an even and an odd part that scatter independently. Far away, the even
solution must be a symmetric combination of free waves, cos⁡(k∣x∣+δe)\cos(k|x| + \delta_e)cos(k∣x∣+δe​), and the odd one an
antisymmetric combination, sgn⁡(x)sin⁡(k∣x∣+δo)\operatorname{sgn}(x)\sin(k|x| + \delta_o)sgn(x)sin(k∣x∣+δo​). The phase shifts δe\delta_eδe​
and δo\delta_oδo​ measure how far the potential shifts each standing wave relative to the free one, for
which both vanish, and they play the role of the partial-wave phase shifts of Chapter 2. Parity
cannot change in the collision, so an even incoming wave produces only an even outgoing wave, and an
odd one only an odd one. In the even/odd basis SSS is therefore diagonal, and by unitarity each
diagonal element is a pure phase. The phase shifts determine these phases. The standing wave
cos⁡(k∣x∣+δe)\cos(k|x| + \delta_e)cos(k∣x∣+δe​) contains the incoming wave e−ik∣x∣e−iδe/2e^{-ik|x|}e^{-i\delta_e}/2e−ik∣x∣e−iδe​/2 and the outgoing wave
eik∣x∣eiδe/2e^{ik|x|}e^{i\delta_e}/2eik∣x∣eiδe​/2, so compared with free motion the potential multiplies the outgoing even
wave by e2iδee^{2i\delta_e}e2iδe​, and in the same way the outgoing odd wave by e2iδoe^{2i\delta_o}e2iδo​. To return to
incidence from the left, we write the scattering
state as a combination Aψe+BψoA\psi_e + B\psi_oAψe​+Bψo​. Requiring that no wave comes in from the right fixes the

t=12(e2iδe+e2iδo),r=12(e2iδe−e2iδo),(M0.14)t = \tfrac12\left(e^{2i\delta_e} + e^{2i\delta_o}\right),\qquad r = \tfrac12\left(e^{2i\delta_e} - e^{2i\delta_o}\right), \tag{M0.14} t=21​(e2iδe​+e2iδo​),r=21​(e2iδe​−e2iδo​),(M0.14)

T=cos⁡2(δe−δo),R=sin⁡2(δe−δo).(M0.15)T = \cos^2(\delta_e - \delta_o),\qquad R = \sin^2(\delta_e - \delta_o). \tag{M0.15} T=cos2(δe​−δo​),R=sin2(δe​−δo​).(M0.15)

A Ramsauer–Townsend resonance is now simply δe=δo\delta_e = \delta_oδe​=δo​ (mod π\piπ): the two channels
produce the same phase, their contributions to the reflected wave cancel, and transmission is complete.

The odd channel is more than a convenient device, because it builds the bridge to three dimensions.
The odd solution vanishes at x=0x = 0x=0, exactly like the s-wave radial function u0(r)u_0(r)u0​(r) at r=0r = 0r=0, and
it obeys the same equation for x>0x > 0x>0. So δo\delta_oδo​ is the s-wave phase shift of the
three-dimensional potential V(r)=V(∣x∣)V(r) = V(|x|)V(r)=V(∣x∣); the test suite checks this numerically. Levinson’s theorem
(Chapter 2, §2.9) carries over: δo(0)=noπ\delta_o(0) = n_o\piδo​(0)=no​π, while the even channel gives
δe(0)=(ne−12)π\delta_e(0) = (n_e - \tfrac12)\piδe​(0)=(ne​−21​)π, where nen_ene​ and non_ono​ count the even and odd bound states. (The
exception is a potential with a state exactly at zero energy, such as V=0V = 0V=0 itself.) The well of
Fig. M0.5 has one bound state of each parity, and indeed δe(0)=π/2\delta_e(0) = \pi/2δe​(0)=π/2 and δo(0)=π\delta_o(0) = \piδo​(0)=π.

M0.7 Wave packets

Stationary states describe a steady beam, but an experiment sends particles one at a time, each of
them localized in space. A single particle is a wave packet, a superposition of plane waves with a
momentum distribution ϕ(k)\phi(k)ϕ(k), and without a potential it evolves as

ψ(x,t)=12π∫ϕ(k) ei(kx−ωt) dk,ℏω=ℏ2k22m.(M0.16)\psi(x,t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int\phi(k)\,e^{i(kx - \omega t)}\,dk, \qquad \hbar\omega = \frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m}. \tag{M0.16} ψ(x,t)=2π​1​∫ϕ(k)ei(kx−ωt)dk,ℏω=2mℏ2k2​.(M0.16)

To see how such a packet moves, suppose that ϕ(k)\phi(k)ϕ(k) is concentrated near a mean wave number k0k_0k0​,
and expand the frequency there, ω(k)≈ω0+v (k−k0)\omega(k) \approx \omega_0 + v\,(k - k_0)ω(k)≈ω0​+v(k−k0​) with v=dω/dkv = d\omega/dkv=dω/dk at
k0k_0k0​. Then

ψ(x,t)≈ei(k0x−ω0t) 12π∫ϕ(k) ei(k−k0)(x−vt) dk,\psi(x,t) \approx e^{i(k_0x - \omega_0t)}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int\phi(k)\,e^{i(k - k_0)(x - vt)}\,dk , ψ(x,t)≈ei(k0​x−ω0​t)2π​1​∫ϕ(k)ei(k−k0​)(x−vt)dk,

a plane wave times an envelope that depends on xxx and ttt only through x−vtx - vtx−vt. The envelope, and
with it the particle, therefore moves with the group velocity v=dω/dk=ℏk0/mv = d\omega/dk = \hbar k_0/mv=dω/dk=ℏk0​/m, the
classical velocity. The next term of the expansion, 12ω′′(k−k0)2\tfrac12\omega''(k - k_0)^221​ω′′(k−k0​)2, makes the packet
spread: a Gaussian packet of initial width σ\sigmaσ grows as σ(t)=σ1+(ℏt/2mσ2)2\sigma(t) = \sigma\sqrt{1 + (\hbar t/2m\sigma^2)^2}σ(t)=σ1+(ℏt/2mσ2)2​
(derivation D.3).

Now let the packet meet a potential. Instead of plane waves we expand it in the stationary scattering

PT=∫∣ϕ(k)∣2 T(k) dk,(M0.17)P_T = \int|\phi(k)|^2\,T(k)\,dk , \tag{M0.17} PT​=∫∣ϕ(k)∣2T(k)dk,(M0.17)

M0.8 Time delay and resonant tunneling

M0.8.1 The Wigner time delay

Transmission probabilities say how likely a particle is to come through, but not when it comes
through. A potential can hold the particle for a while, and this information sits in the phase of the
transmission amplitude, which (M0.17) discards. Write t(k)=∣t∣ eiφ(k)t(k) = |t|\,e^{i\varphi(k)}t(k)=∣t∣eiφ(k), with the phase
referred to free propagation, so that t=1t = 1t=1 without a potential. The transmitted packet is then
∫ϕ ∣t∣ ei[kx−ωt+φ(k)] dk\int\phi\,|t|\,e^{i[kx - \omega t + \varphi(k)]}\,dk∫ϕ∣t∣ei[kx−ωt+φ(k)]dk. As in §M0.7, its centre lies where the phase of
the integrand is stationary in kkk at k0k_0k0​, that is where x−vt+dφ/dk=0x - vt + d\varphi/dk = 0x−vt+dφ/dk=0. Compared with a
free packet, which is at x=vtx = vtx=vt, the transmitted packet is displaced by −dφ/dk-d\varphi/dk−dφ/dk, and therefore
arrives late by

τW=1vdφdk=ℏ dφdE,(M0.18)\tau_W = \frac{1}{v}\frac{d\varphi}{dk} = \hbar\,\frac{d\varphi}{dE}, \tag{M0.18} τW​=v1​dkdφ​=ℏdEdφ​,(M0.18)

the Wigner time delay (the second form uses dE=ℏv dkdE = \hbar v\,dkdE=ℏvdk). It can be negative: the
transmitted packet is then built mainly from the front of the incident one and seems to arrive early.
This reshaping does not violate causality.

M0.8.2 Double barriers and resonant tunneling

The delay becomes large when the potential can trap the particle. Put two barriers around a well. The
inner well then has quasi-bound states, which would be bound states if the barriers were infinitely
thick and which, for barriers of finite thickness, leak out through them. When the energy matches one
of these states, a symmetric double barrier becomes perfectly transparent, even if each barrier
alone transmits only a few percent. This is resonant tunneling, the principle of the
resonant-tunneling diode, and a one-dimensional model of the nuclear shape resonances of Chapter 2.

The form of the transmission near such a state follows from its decay. If the probability of
finding the particle in the well decays as e−Γt/ℏe^{-\Gamma t/\hbar}e−Γt/ℏ, the amplitude decays as
e−Γt/2ℏe^{-\Gamma t/2\hbar}e−Γt/2ℏ, and that is the time dependence e−iEt/ℏe^{-iEt/\hbar}e−iEt/ℏ of a state with the complex
energy E=Er−iΓ/2E = E_r - i\Gamma/2E=Er​−iΓ/2. The scattering amplitudes, continued to complex energies, have a pole
there (Chapter 8 makes this precise). Near a narrow, isolated
resonance this pole dominates the energy dependence of ttt, which is then proportional to
(Γ/2)/(E−Er+iΓ/2)(\Gamma/2)/(E - E_r + i\Gamma/2)(Γ/2)/(E−Er​+iΓ/2). The transmission is the probability of entering the well through
the left barrier times that of leaving it through the right one, T=ΓLΓR/[(E−Er)2+(Γ/2)2]T = \Gamma_L\Gamma_R/[(E - E_r)^2 + (\Gamma/2)^2]T=ΓL​ΓR​/[(E−Er​)2+(Γ/2)2]
with Γ=ΓL+ΓR\Gamma = \Gamma_L + \Gamma_RΓ=ΓL​+ΓR​. For a symmetric double barrier ΓL=ΓR=Γ/2\Gamma_L = \Gamma_R = \Gamma/2ΓL​=ΓR​=Γ/2, and
three properties follow. The transmission is a Lorentzian that reaches 1 at the peak. The phase of the
pole factor, arctan⁡[2(E−Er)/Γ]\arctan[2(E - E_r)/\Gamma]arctan[2(E−Er​)/Γ] up to a constant, rises by π\piπ across the resonance. And
its derivative at the peak, 2/Γ2/\Gamma2/Γ, gives through (M0.18) the delay:

T(E)≈(Γ/2)2(E−Er)2+(Γ/2)2,φ rises by π,τW(Er)=2ℏΓ.(M0.19)T(E) \approx \frac{(\Gamma/2)^2}{(E - E_r)^2 + (\Gamma/2)^2}, \qquad \varphi \text{ rises by } \pi, \qquad \tau_W(E_r) = \frac{2\hbar}{\Gamma}. \tag{M0.19} T(E)≈(E−Er​)2+(Γ/2)2(Γ/2)2​,φ rises by π,τW​(Er​)=Γ2ℏ​.(M0.19)

The width Γ\GammaΓ sets the lifetime ℏ/Γ\hbar/\Gammaℏ/Γ of the quasi-bound state, and the time delay at the
peak is twice that.

Our double barrier (height 4, width 0.75, well width 4.2, in units ℏ=2m=1\hbar = 2m = 1ℏ=2m=1) has three
resonances below its top (Table M0.1).

reproduces the measured delays to 0.2 time units. On the resonance the delay is 10.5, slightly less

M0.9 Numerical toolkit: transfer matrices and split-operator propagation

M0.9.1 Transfer matrices

The closed forms of this chapter cover a few special shapes. A general one-dimensional potential can be
treated by cutting the xxx-axis into layers in which the potential is constant, VjV_jVj​ in layer jjj. In
each layer the solution is Ajeikjx+Bje−ikjxA_je^{ik_jx} + B_je^{-ik_jx}Aj​eikj​x+Bj​e−ikj​x, with kj=2m(E−Vj)/ℏk_j = \sqrt{2m(E - V_j)}/\hbarkj​=2m(E−Vj​)​/ℏ, which is
imaginary in forbidden layers. At the edge xjx_jxj​ between layers jjj and j+1j + 1j+1, the solution and its
derivative must be continuous:

Ajeikjxj+Bje−ikjxj=Aj+1eikj+1xj+Bj+1e−ikj+1xj,kj(Ajeikjxj−Bje−ikjxj)=kj+1(Aj+1eikj+1xj−Bj+1e−ikj+1xj).\begin{aligned} A_je^{ik_jx_j} + B_je^{-ik_jx_j} &= A_{j+1}e^{ik_{j+1}x_j} + B_{j+1}e^{-ik_{j+1}x_j},\\ k_j\big(A_je^{ik_jx_j} - B_je^{-ik_jx_j}\big) &= k_{j+1}\big(A_{j+1}e^{ik_{j+1}x_j} - B_{j+1}e^{-ik_{j+1}x_j}\big). \end{aligned} Aj​eikj​xj​+Bj​e−ikj​xj​kj​(Aj​eikj​xj​−Bj​e−ikj​xj​)​=Aj+1​eikj+1​xj​+Bj+1​e−ikj+1​xj​,=kj+1​(Aj+1​eikj+1​xj​−Bj+1​e−ikj+1​xj​).​

Dividing the second equation by kj+1k_{j+1}kj+1​, and adding it to the first or subtracting it from the first,
isolates Aj+1A_{j+1}Aj+1​ and Bj+1B_{j+1}Bj+1​. With ρj=kj/kj+1\rho_j = k_j/k_{j+1}ρj​=kj​/kj+1​ the result is a 2×22\times22×2 matrix that
carries the amplitudes across the edge:

(Aj+1Bj+1)=12((1+ρj) ei(kj−kj+1)xj(1−ρj) e−i(kj+kj+1)xj(1−ρj) ei(kj+kj+1)xj(1+ρj) e−i(kj−kj+1)xj)(AjBj),ρj=kjkj+1.(M0.20)\begin{pmatrix} A_{j+1} \\ B_{j+1} \end{pmatrix} = \frac12 \begin{pmatrix} (1 + \rho_j)\,e^{i(k_j - k_{j+1})x_j} & (1 - \rho_j)\,e^{-i(k_j + k_{j+1})x_j} \\ (1 - \rho_j)\,e^{i(k_j + k_{j+1})x_j} & (1 + \rho_j)\,e^{-i(k_j - k_{j+1})x_j} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} A_j \\ B_j \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \rho_j = \frac{k_j}{k_{j+1}} . \tag{M0.20} (Aj+1​Bj+1​​)=21​((1+ρj​)ei(kj​−kj+1​)xj​(1−ρj​)ei(kj​+kj+1​)xj​​(1−ρj​)e−i(kj​+kj+1​)xj​(1+ρj​)e−i(kj​−kj+1​)xj​​)(Aj​Bj​​),ρj​=kj+1​kj​​.(M0.20)

The product of these matrices over all edges, MMM, links the first layer to the last,
(AN,BN)=M (A0,B0)(A_N, B_N) = M\,(A_0, B_0)(AN​,BN​)=M(A0​,B0​). Incidence from the left means (A0,B0)=(1,r)(A_0, B_0) = (1, r)(A0​,B0​)=(1,r) and
(AN,BN)=(t,0)(A_N, B_N) = (t, 0)(AN​,BN​)=(t,0). The second component of this relation, 0=M21+M22r0 = M_{21} + M_{22}r0=M21​+M22​r, gives rrr; the
first, t=M11+M12rt = M_{11} + M_{12}rt=M11​+M12​r, then gives t=(M11M22−M12M21)/M22=det⁡M/M22t = (M_{11}M_{22} - M_{12}M_{21})/M_{22} = \det M/M_{22}t=(M11​M22​−M12​M21​)/M22​=detM/M22​. Each
edge matrix has the determinant 14[(1+ρj)2−(1−ρj)2]=ρj\frac14[(1 + \rho_j)^2 - (1 - \rho_j)^2] = \rho_j41​[(1+ρj​)2−(1−ρj​)2]=ρj​, so the product
det⁡M=∏jkj/kj+1\det M = \prod_j k_j/k_{j+1}detM=∏j​kj​/kj+1​ telescopes to k0/kNk_0/k_Nk0​/kN​, and

r=−M21M22,t=det⁡MM22=k0kN 1M22.(M0.21)r = -\frac{M_{21}}{M_{22}},\qquad t = \frac{\det M}{M_{22}} = \frac{k_0}{k_N}\,\frac{1}{M_{22}} . \tag{M0.21} r=−M22​M21​​,t=M22​detM​=kN​k0​​M22​1​.(M0.21)

The method is exact for layered potentials (Fig. M0.2). A smooth potential must be approximated by a
staircase, and the error then falls as 1/n21/n^21/n2 with the number nnn of slices (Fig. M0.8(a)). For very
thick barriers the matrix elements grow like eκae^{\kappa a}eκa and eventually overflow; composing S-matrices
instead of transfer matrices cures this, but we will not need it.

M0.9.2 The split-operator method

To follow a packet in time we must apply the evolution operator e−iHΔt/ℏe^{-iH\Delta t/\hbar}e−iHΔt/ℏ again and again,
with H=T+VH = T + VH=T+V. Each part alone is easy to apply: the kinetic energy TTT is diagonal in momentum
space, where it is a multiplication by ℏ2k2/2m\hbar^2k^2/2mℏ2k2/2m, and the potential is diagonal in position space.
The two parts do not commute, however, so e−iHΔt/ℏe^{-iH\Delta t/\hbar}e−iHΔt/ℏ is not simply the product of the two
exponentials; by the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula, the error of the plain product is of order
Δt2\Delta t^2Δt2, coming from the commutator [T,V][T, V][T,V]. The symmetric arrangement

e−iHΔt/ℏ≈e−iVΔt/2ℏ  e−iTΔt/ℏ  e−iVΔt/2ℏ(M0.22)e^{-iH\Delta t/\hbar} \approx e^{-iV\Delta t/2\hbar}\;e^{-iT\Delta t/\hbar}\;e^{-iV\Delta t/2\hbar} \tag{M0.22} e−iHΔt/ℏ≈e−iVΔt/2ℏe−iTΔt/ℏe−iVΔt/2ℏ(M0.22)

cancels that term and leaves an error of order Δt3\Delta t^3Δt3 per step (derivation D.4), hence of order
Δt2\Delta t^2Δt2 after a fixed time. The middle factor is applied by a fast Fourier transform to momentum
space and back. Every factor is unitary, so the norm is conserved exactly. The grid is periodic, so
outgoing waves must be removed before they wrap around; a mask that falls smoothly to zero near the
grid ends does this.

Two pitfalls showed up while preparing this chapter, and both concern the comparison between
time-dependent and stationary calculations. The first is that one must compare like with like. On a
grid, a barrier occupies whole cells, so a barrier of width 1 on a grid of step 0.073 is really 0.95
wide, and that alone changes TTT by 2–3 %. A stationary comparison must therefore use the potential
exactly as the grid represents it (od.grid_layers), or the edges must be placed on cell boundaries,
as in this notebook. The second concerns the time step. The method is stable for any Δt\Delta tΔt, but
sharp edges scatter a little probability into the highest momenta the grid can hold, and a large step
propagates these components wrongly. When the true transmission is small, they spoil it. In
Fig. M0.8(b), with T≈8×10−3T \approx 8\times10^{-3}T≈8×10−3, the error is 20 % at Δt=0.08\Delta t = 0.08Δt=0.08 and below 1.5 % for
Δt≲dx2/2\Delta t \lesssim dx^2/2Δt≲dx2/2; in other set-ups the error went the other way and reached a factor of four.
The rule of thumb, in physical units, is Δt≲m dx2/ℏ\Delta t \lesssim m\,dx^2/\hbarΔt≲mdx2/ℏ.

Figure M0.8. (a) Error of the staircase approximation of the Eckart barrier against the number
of slices. (b) Transmission of a packet through the double barrier at E0=0.8E_0 = 0.8E0​=0.8, relative to the
stationary prediction, against the time step. (Notebook §M0.9.)

Summary

A one-dimensional scattering problem is fixed by its asymptotic form, an incident wave of unit
amplitude together with a reflected wave rrr and a transmitted wave ttt, and because the probability
current is the same everywhere in a stationary state, the reflection and transmission probabilities
add up to one, provided TTT is defined as a ratio of fluxes. The exactly solvable potentials showed
that a quantum particle is reflected by any abrupt change of the potential, even above a step, and
that it can cross a barrier it could not cross classically. Through a rectangular barrier the
transmission falls as e−2κae^{-2\kappa a}e−2κa, and the same reasoning applied slice by slice to a smooth
barrier gives the Gamow factor e−2Ge^{-2G}e−2G, which the Hill–Wheeler formula refines near the barrier top.
With no adjustable parameter, this picture explains why α-decay half-lives range over 24 orders of
magnitude. Interference makes wells and barriers perfectly transparent at special energies, and the
S-matrix that organizes all these amplitudes is unitary because flux is conserved and symmetric
because of time reversal; for a symmetric potential it is diagonal in the even and odd channels, with
T=cos⁡2(δe−δo)T = \cos^2(\delta_e - \delta_o)T=cos2(δe​−δo​), and the odd phase shift is exactly the s-wave phase shift of
Chapter 2. Wave packets give the stationary quantities their meaning: a packet splits with the
probabilities of the packet-averaged TTT, its transmitted part is filtered towards higher energies, and
it arrives late by the Wigner time ℏ dφ/dE\hbar\,d\varphi/dEℏdφ/dE, which reaches 2ℏ/Γ2\hbar/\Gamma2ℏ/Γ on a resonance
of width Γ\GammaΓ. Transfer matrices and split-operator propagation reproduce all of these results,
as long as stationary and time-dependent calculations use the same discretized potential and a small
enough time step.

Detailed derivation

Several results above were derived only in outline, so as not to interrupt the argument. This
section gives the complete algebra, in the order in which the results appear in the chapter.

D.1 The Gamow integral for a Coulomb barrier

Section M0.4.3 needs the integral (M0.9) for the barrier that an α particle of energy QQQ sees outside
a daughter nucleus of charge ZdZ_dZd​. Beyond the nuclear radius RRR the potential is V(r)=2Zde2/rV(r) = 2Z_de^2/rV(r)=2Zd​e2/r,
and the outer turning point bbb, where V(b)=QV(b) = QV(b)=Q, is b=2Zde2/Qb = 2Z_de^2/Qb=2Zd​e2/Q. Writing V(r)−Q=Q (b/r−1)V(r) - Q = Q\,(b/r - 1)V(r)−Q=Q(b/r−1),
the Gamow integral becomes

G=2μQℏ∫Rbbr−1  dr.G = \frac{\sqrt{2\mu Q}}{\hbar}\int_R^b\sqrt{\frac{b}{r} - 1}\;dr . G=ℏ2μQ​​∫Rb​rb​−1​dr.

The square root suggests the substitution r=bcos⁡2θr = b\cos^2\thetar=bcos2θ, for which b/r−1=tan⁡2θb/r - 1 = \tan^2\thetab/r−1=tan2θ and
dr=−2bcos⁡θsin⁡θ dθdr = -2b\cos\theta\sin\theta\,d\thetadr=−2bcosθsinθdθ. The upper limit r=br = br=b becomes θ=0\theta = 0θ=0, and the lower
limit r=Rr = Rr=R becomes θ0=arccos⁡x\theta_0 = \arccos\sqrt{x}θ0​=arccosx​, with x=R/bx = R/bx=R/b. The integrand turns into
tan⁡θ⋅2bcos⁡θsin⁡θ=2bsin⁡2θ\tan\theta \cdot 2b\cos\theta\sin\theta = 2b\sin^2\thetatanθ⋅2bcosθsinθ=2bsin2θ, so

∫Rbbr−1  dr=2b∫0θ0sin⁡2θ dθ=b (θ0−sin⁡θ0cos⁡θ0)=b[arccos⁡x−x(1−x)],\int_R^b\sqrt{\frac{b}{r} - 1}\;dr = 2b\int_0^{\theta_0}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta = b\,\big(\theta_0 - \sin\theta_0\cos\theta_0\big) = b\left[\arccos\sqrt{x} - \sqrt{x(1 - x)}\right], ∫Rb​rb​−1​dr=2b∫0θ0​​sin2θdθ=b(θ0​−sinθ0​cosθ0​)=b[arccosx​−x(1−x)​],

which is (M0.12). For a small nucleus, x≪1x \ll 1x≪1, the expansion arccos⁡x≈π/2−x\arccos\sqrt{x} \approx \pi/2 - \sqrt{x}arccosx​≈π/2−x​
gives the bracket π/2−2x\pi/2 - 2\sqrt{x}π/2−2x​. The leading term,
2G≈πb2μQ/ℏ=2πZde22μ/Q/ℏ2G \approx \pi b\sqrt{2\mu Q}/\hbar = 2\pi Z_de^2\sqrt{2\mu/Q}/\hbar2G≈πb2μQ​/ℏ=2πZd​e22μ/Q​/ℏ, is exactly 2πη2\pi\eta2πη, with the
Sommerfeld parameter η=2Zde2/ℏv\eta = 2Z_de^2/\hbar vη=2Zd​e2/ℏv of the α particle, whose velocity is v=2Q/μv = \sqrt{2Q/\mu}v=2Q/μ​. The
Gamow factor of a pure Coulomb barrier is therefore e−2πηe^{-2\pi\eta}e−2πη, the same factor that M1 finds in
the Coulomb wave functions (eq. M1.32).

ψ=Aψe+Bψo\psi = A\psi_e + B\psi_oψ=Aψe​+Bψo​, where far away ψe=cos⁡(k∣x∣+δe)\psi_e = \cos(k|x| + \delta_e)ψe​=cos(k∣x∣+δe​) and

D.3 Spreading of a Gaussian packet

Take a packet centred at x=0x = 0x=0 whose probability density is a Gaussian of standard deviation
